newsitem.title: USA: Cambodia coup could complicate U.S. Asia policy.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia coup could complicate U.S. Asia policy.

text.p: Just as President Bill Clinton basks in the success of NATO's decision to expand, a coup in Cambodia has raised new questions about his leadership and could complicate his Asia policy for a long time.

The United States, which played a lead role in the 1991 treaty that brought fleeting peace to Cambodia, is putting its faith in fresh diplomatic efforts to keep the country from renewed civil war but officials admit the strategy is unlikely to succeed and they apparently have no firm backup plan.
"It's very important that we give diplomacy a chance ... to see if there's any way that the 1991 (peace) accords can be preserved," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

He acknowledged, however, that based on Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's unyielding assertion of power in Phnom Penh and his violent crackdown against political opponents, "Hun Sen appears to not be interested in any kind of reasonable compromise."

Critics said despite investing billions of dollars in aid, the United States and other Western governments paid little attention to Cambodia after declaring success in encouraging democracy there with the 1991 peace treaty and 1993 elections.

The recent announced expansion of the NATO alliance to include Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic represented a diplomatic triumph for Clinton. But his administration is under fire for failing to oppose the power-sharing arrangement under which Hun Sen gained a leadership position even though his party lost the 1993 polls to Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
It was Ranarridh, the first prime minister, whom Hun Sen ousted with military force last Sunday. Hun Sen has superior military clout but apparently feared an election loss in 1998.
"Cambodia represents a failure of the Clinton administration's leadership in Asia," said Asia expert Richard Fisher of the conservative Heritage Foundation.
Washington "tried to build better relations with Hun Sen instead of using its leverage over U.S. and international aid to curb his abuses and strengthen democratic leaders," he said.
As tensions grew between Hun Sen and Ranariddh, Washington felt an armed overthrow by Hun Sen was possible, but not necessarily inevitable, U.S. officials said.

They insisted there were no regrets that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on a trip to Asia two weeks ago, skipped a stop to Phnom Penh, where -- face to face -- she could have urged Hun Sen and Ranariddh to keep their peace treaty vows.
Along with the security risk, "the sense among her party was that even if she went there, it was not clear that her visit would make a difference," one official said.

Fisher considers it a "critical error" that Albright did not, at that key point, personally deliver a strong message to Cambodian leaders. If security was a concern, she could have brought "a planeload of marines," he said.
Republican Representative Dana Rohrabacher of California agreed. He said: "Albright could have had an influence, if she went to Cambodia, on this bully (Hun Sen) because she's a pretty tough gal."

Ranariddh, aiming to build international support for sanctions against Hun Sen, was welcomed at the State Department on Friday as Cambodia's elected leader. Nevertheless, officials continue to deal with Hun Sen, whom they consider Cambodia's brightest and most effective, albeit ruthless, politician.

"There are no heroes here ... There have been mistakes all around the political spectrum in Cambodia," including by Ranariddh who toyed with a political alliance with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group responsible for more than one million deaths when it ruled Cambodia in 1975-1979, Burns said.
Washington wants the ruling coalition reinstated but officials say Ranariddh, due to enmity with Hun Sen, likely must be replaced. A successor is not obvious.
Officials say they are not considering military options.

The hope is that a united effort by the Association of Southeastern Asian Nations to isolate Cambodia and at least a temporary suspension of some aid will force Hun Sen to deal. If not, the United States may have to consider backing a total aid halt and tough sanctions as it seeks to ensure Cambodia does not undermine its broader Asia policy.
